notes: Hand-labeled from the video's manual English captions. gold = [start_s, end_s] spans where the answer is said. keywords = regex groups (lowercased); the answer evidence is present only when EVERY group matches the retrieved text. reference = the answer an LLM judge grades against. Unanswerable questions are not covered anywhere in the talk.

questions.question: According to his formula, what determines the quality of your communication, and which factor matters least?
questions.reference: Knowledge, practice and inherent talent (K, P and T), where talent (T) is the small factor; knowledge matters most.

questions.question: Which Olympic athlete did he see skiing at Sun Valley?
questions.reference: Mary Lou Retton, the Olympic gymnast.

questions.question: What share of an audience is fogged out at any given moment?
questions.reference: About 20%.

questions.question: How long can a speaker wait for an answer after asking the audience a question?
questions.reference: About seven seconds.

questions.question: What is the best time of day to give a lecture?
questions.reference: 11 AM.

questions.question: What does he imagine the empty seats are filled with before a talk?
questions.reference: Disinterested farm animals.

questions.question: How full should the lecture room be?
questions.reference: It doesn't have to be packed, but more than half full.

questions.question: Which play does he use to show how playwrights use props, and what was the prop?
questions.reference: Ibsen's Hedda Gabler; the manuscript that ends up in the potbellied stove's fire.

questions.question: Which instructor let a steel-ball pendulum swing back to his own nose?
questions.reference: Alan Lazarus, in 8.01, demonstrating conservation of energy.

questions.question: What minimum font size do they settle on for slides?
questions.reference: About 40 or 50; 35 is starting to get too small.

questions.question: What is a hapax legomenon slide?
questions.reference: A slide you can get away with exactly once per presentation, like the impossibly complex Afghanistan diagram.

questions.question: How long does a faculty job candidate have to show vision and that they've done something?
questions.reference: Five minutes.

questions.question: What did Julia Child say when asked whether it is fun to be famous?
questions.reference: "You get used to it," adding that you never get used to being ignored.

questions.question: What slogan was attached to his arch-learning thesis work?
questions.reference: One-shot learning.

questions.question: How many books had Delores Etter written compared with him?
questions.reference: She had written 21 books; he had written 17.

questions.question: How did the old Latin mass signal that it was over?
questions.reference: It ended with "ite missa est": the mass is over, you can go home now.

questions.question: Why does he advise against opening a talk with a joke, and what should you open with instead?
questions.reference: At the start people are still settling in and adjusting to your voice, so jokes fall flat; open with an empowerment promise of what they will know by the end.

questions.question: Why does he ban laptops and cell phones during his talk?
questions.reference: Humans have only one language processor, so browsing or email distracts you, distracts people around you, and an open laptop makes him do a worse job.

questions.question: What are the advantages of teaching with a blackboard?
questions.reference: Graphic quality, writing speed that matches how fast people absorb ideas, and a target for your hands to point at.

questions.question: How does the duct tape trick settle which way the spinning bicycle wheel turns?
questions.reference: Think only about the small piece of wheel under the duct tape: blowing on it as it comes over the top pushes it sideways, and each piece does the same, so the wheel turns that way. It is thinking about the problem the right way.

questions.question: Why does he think chalk and props work better than slides?
questions.reference: Empathetic mirroring: watching someone write on the board or handle a prop activates your mirror neurons so you feel yourself doing it, which a slide or picture can't do.

questions.question: What is wrong with using a laser pointer, and what should you do instead?
questions.reference: You must turn your head to point, losing eye contact and engagement with the audience; instead put a numbered arrow on the slide and refer to it.

questions.question: What did his survey find inspires students and faculty?
questions.reference: Freshmen were inspired by a teacher who said they could do it, senior faculty by someone who helped them see a problem in a new way, and everyone by someone showing passion for their work.

questions.question: How does he say you teach people how to think?
questions.reference: We are storytelling animals, so give people the stories they need, the questions to ask about them, and ways to analyze, combine and evaluate stories.

questions.question: What are the elements of Winston's star for getting your work remembered?
questions.reference: Symbol, slogan, surprise, salient idea and story.

questions.question: Why is ending a talk with "thank you" a weak move?
questions.reference: It suggests the audience stayed only out of politeness and wanted to be elsewhere; you can mouth thank you once applause starts, but it shouldn't be your last move.
